phrase: You buy bitcoin at the price you deserve
note: A popular Bitcoin saying: the price you pay reflects how early you understood it. Missing out, or selling too soon, is the cost of learning late.

phrase: For the tuition you earned
note: 'Paying tuition' is trader slang for losing money while learning how markets work. The lesson is expensive but, ideally, you only pay it once.

phrase: We saw the dot com bubble that bursted
note: In the late 1990s investors poured money into internet start-ups. When the bubble burst from 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq lost nearly 80% and many companies vanished.

phrase: And that’s a zero sum game
note: In a zero-sum game one player's gain is exactly another's loss. Chasing paper profits can work that way: digits change hands, nothing new is created.

phrase: It’s too big to fail
note: 'Too big to fail' describes banks so large that governments rescue them rather than let them collapse, as in the 2008 bailouts. Bitcoin's first block quotes a headline about a bank bailout.

phrase:
Might sell with sell pressure
But no liquidity
note: Sell pressure is a wave of people trying to sell. Liquidity is how easily you can sell without crashing the price. When liquidity dries up, sellers find no buyers at fair prices.

phrase: Are straight up owners of debt
note: In a debt-based system, lenders and bondholders get paid first. When companies fail, creditors are repaid before shareholders, and savers holding cash lose value to inflation.

phrase: Commercial lien that’s a fatal error
note: A lien is a legal claim over someone's property until a debt is paid. Miss the payments and the lender can seize the asset: you own it only until you don't.

phrase: Hate the game and still a player
note: A twist on 'don't hate the player, hate the game'. You can dislike the fiat money system and still live inside it, so learn its rules and play it better.

phrase: Money don’t grow on trees
note: The history of money, from metal to paper to digital, runs through the 'Saylor Series': 17 long conversations between Michael Saylor and Robert Breedlove on the What is Money? podcast.

phrase: Before that, pressed out of metal
note: For thousands of years money was metal: gold, silver and copper coins. The earliest known coins were struck in Lydia, in modern-day Turkey, more than 2,500 years ago.

phrase: Pressed ink on paper sheets
note: Metal is heavy to carry, so banks issued paper notes as claims on the coins and gold in their vaults. Paper became a stand-in for the real thing.

phrase: Promissory notes were great receipts
note: A promissory note is a written promise to pay. Early banknotes were exactly that: receipts redeemable for gold or silver on demand, until governments ended the link.

phrase: Until the bank run made them see
note: A bank run is when many depositors withdraw at once, fearing the bank can't pay. Banks lend out most deposits, so they never hold enough cash to repay everyone at the same time.

phrase: Restricted access, leaky faucet
note: Money held by someone else can be frozen or limited: restricted access. Inflation is the leaky faucet, value dripping out of savings so slowly most people never notice.

phrase: Insurance don’t cover pyramid below
note: A pyramid scheme pays early members with money from later ones and collapses when new money stops. Critics argue debt-based money has a similar shape, with the most exposed at the bottom.

phrase: From penthouse down when the hotel floods
note: New money enters the economy at the top, through banks and asset owners, before reaching everyone else. Economists call it the Cantillon effect: those first in line gain while the floors below absorb the damage.

phrase: Don’t wanna let that sink in
note: In October 2022, Elon Musk walked into Twitter's San Francisco headquarters carrying a bathroom sink, posting 'let that sink in!' days before closing his US$44 billion purchase of the company, now X.

phrase: Quick realize paddler missing
note: A twist on 'up the creek without a paddle': stuck in trouble with no way to steer. Lose your savings in a crisis and you're adrift.

phrase: They did me like how they reboot yeezy
note: A nod to an internet conspiracy theory, mostly a meme, claiming Kanye West (Ye) was secretly replaced by a clone or body double. There is no evidence for it.

phrase:
Where’s my money?
It’s in the vault
note: A bank vault holds only a small fraction of what depositors are owed. Most of 'your' money is a number in the bank's books, already lent out to someone else.

phrase:
Can I get it out now
Maybe tomorrow
note: Australian banks can make cash slow to reach: branches may need notice for large withdrawals, ATMs cap daily amounts, and staff may ask why you want your own money, citing scam and money-laundering checks.

phrase: You know it’s my money
note: The Bitcoin answer is self-custody: hold your own keys and no teller, branch or policy can say 'maybe tomorrow'. Be your own bank.
